title: Debt and contentment
hookLine: contentment guards against spending beyond means
tomorrow: Bebe hands Simran an empty envelope. what's it for?

cards: A checkout page with a soft little button under the price: pay in four easy installments. Simran's first full paycheck has just landed, and the headphones she's wanted all year are sitting in her cart.
They cost more than the whole check. But four easy payments. It doesn't feel like debt.
It feels like a discount. Her thumb hovers over the button.

teach.b: One question today: what keeps a want from spending money you don't have yet? The Sikh answer is santokh, contentment. In the Japji, Guru Nanak takes an old picture, a bull holding up the earth, and turns it.
In paraphrase: the bull is dharma, the son of compassion, and contentment is what holds the earth patiently in place. So contentment isn't laziness or giving up. It's what holds things steady.
A person with santokh still works, still earns, still wants things. They just don't let this month's want borrow from next month. Now a neighbor who says something close.
Buddhists read in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "contentedness the best riches."
That's the shared thing: being content is itself a kind of wealth, and no checkout button can sell it to you. And the honest difference.
In that Dhammapada verse, contentedness stands beside nirvana, on a path that, for Buddhist monks and nuns, means leaving a household behind.
In the Japji, santokh is set in a working world: the bull holds up the earth where people farm, trade and raise families, and where Simran keeps her job at the stall.
Two homes for one word, and neither needs the other to be wrong. Simran closes the tab. She'll save for the headphones, and buy them when the money is actually hers.

how: Sikhs speak of santokh, contentment, as a virtue of the householder: working and earning while living within one's means. Japji, where it appears, is part of the daily morning prayers.

o: a loan the gurdwara gives to members in need
a fast kept until all your old debts are paid
contentment that stops spending beyond your means

games.q: enough, in two traditions — tap the pairs.
p: a want borrowing from next month

s: santokh means giving up work and wanting nothing
a person with santokh still works and wants; they just don't let a want borrow from next month.
in Max Müller's Dhammapada, contentedness is called the best riches
the shared thing: being content is itself a kind of wealth.
the Sikh and Buddhist lines mean exactly the same thing
they share contentment as wealth; the Dhammapada sets it beside nirvana, the Japji in a working, householding world.

games.q: your brother wants a new gaming laptop on a store card. his old one works fine. what does santokh say?
o: save for it; don't let this month's want borrow from next month.
never want anything new; the wanting itself is the problem.
buy it; he works hard, and everybody carries a little debt.
games.why: santokh isn't wanting nothing; it holds things steady. Simran closed the tab and is saving for the headphones.

practice: Count, slowly, five things you already have that are enough as they are: a jacket that still keeps you warm, a phone that still works, a friend who still answers. One breath for each. Then sit with the count.

wordCard.voice: Debt and contentment. Santokh holds you steady, so a want doesn't borrow from next month.

carryVoice: Your line: enough. Contentment holds the earth, and it can hold a paycheck too. Until next time.

sources.ref: Japji, pauri 16, Ang 3 (dhaul dharam daiaa ka poot, santokh thaap rakhiaa jin soot), paraphrased
